warmup.q: The payments database runs on a main computer, and a copy follows it about 50 ms behind. By default, the main computer tells the app "saved" as soon as a payment is on its own disk. At 10:42:07 its disk dies, and a minute later someone turns the copy into the new main computer. What happened to the payments the app was told were saved at 10:42:06.98?
options: They're on the copy: the database says "saved" only once the copy has them
They're probably lost: they were saved only on the dead disk, and the last 50 ms of changes never reached the copy
They're lost only if someone was reading from the copy at that moment
When the copy takes over, it fetches them from the dead computer's disk
warmup.why: This is the asynchronous failover of One leader, many followers (lesson 1), on a real system. By default, PostgreSQL answers a commit once the change is on the main computer's own disk, and sends it to the copy a moment later. Payments saved inside that moment exist only on the dead disk, so the copy never sees them, although the app was told they were saved. The first option is the trap: only a synchronous copy, which the second section sets up, closes that gap. And a copy that takes over replays only what it already received; it can't reach into a dead machine.

sections.h: Building a standby: a copy that replays the primary's log
sections.html:
Let's build the copy from the opening. PostgreSQL is a free database program that many companies run, and one running PostgreSQL is called a server. A server keeps its data in one folder, the data directory, in files cut into 8 KB pages.

Before PostgreSQL changes a page, it adds a note of the change to the end of the write-ahead log (WAL), a file it only ever appends to. If the server crashes, it goes back to the last checkpoint, a moment when every change so far had reached the data files, and replays each note written after it. That replay is crash recovery. (The Storage engines track's lesson Write-ahead logging and crash recovery builds this.)

Now take a copy of the data directory and never let its recovery end. Keep feeding it the main server's WAL as the main server writes it, and the copy replays each note onto the same pages. That copy is a standby, and the server it follows is the primary. It's a copy byte for byte: the same pages, the same row positions, and the same major version, the first number in a version such as 18.1.

Picture the café's notebook of payments, with a photocopy kept in another town. Each new line is read out over the phone and written into the copy. The notebook is the WAL, the phone line is the network, and the copy is the standby. The picture breaks where the opening did: a standby copies bytes, not meaning, so it copies a mistake as faithfully as a payment.

One command builds a standby, and the file that starts this lesson's servers, env/postgres-ha.yml, uses it. Three of its options matter:

  • pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D $PGDATA -X stream -S standby1 -R copies the running primary's data directory over the network, plus the WAL written while it copies (-X stream). It logs in as replicator, a user that the primary's pg_hba.conf, its list of who may connect from where, allows to replicate.
  • -R writes an empty file, standby.signal, which makes the server start as a standby and stay in recovery. It also writes primary_conninfo, how to reach the primary (its address, user and password), into postgresql.auto.conf.
  • -S standby1 streams through a replication slot, a note on the primary of the oldest WAL this standby still needs, its restart_lsn.

Once started, the standby runs a process (a running program) called the walreceiver, which connects to the primary, and the primary starts a walsender to serve it. The walsender sends WAL as soon as it's written. The walreceiver writes it into the standby's own WAL folder, pg_wal, and forces it onto the disk with fsync, the call that waits until the disk really holds the bytes. Then the standby's startup process replays it. A place in the WAL is an LSN (log sequence number), a count of bytes from the start of the log, printed like 0/508F830. pg_wal_lsn_diff subtracts two of them and gives the distance in bytes.

The slot matters when a standby stops. Without one, the primary deletes old WAL files, called segments, at each checkpoint, once its own crash recovery no longer needs it, whether a standby has read it or not. A standby that was down too long then gets requested WAL segment ... has already been removed, and must be built again from a fresh copy. With a slot, the primary keeps all WAL from restart_lsn on.

That's also the danger. A slot whose standby is gone for good keeps WAL forever, until pg_wal fills the disk and the primary stops. So drop slots you no longer use. And set max_slot_wal_keep_size (default -1, no limit) or PostgreSQL 18's idle_replication_slot_timeout (default 0, off), so the primary gives up on a slot before the disk gives up on the primary. With the standby stopped and the timeout at 10 seconds, the next checkpoint gave up on the slot:

 slot_name | active | wal_status | invalidation_reason
-----------+--------+------------+---------------------
 standby1  | f      | lost       | idle_timeout

-- the standby's log when it came back
FATAL:  could not start WAL streaming: ERROR:  can no longer access replication slot "standby1"
DETAIL:  This replication slot has been invalidated due to "idle_timeout".

On the primary, the view pg_stat_replication, a built-in table you can query, has one row per standby with three positions, and the figure shows where each is measured. write_lsn is WAL the standby has handed to its operating system (the program that runs all the others), which may still hold it in memory. flush_lsn is WAL on the standby's disk. replay_lsn is what queries on the standby can see. write_lag, flush_lag and replay_lag give the same distances in time.

The standby follows a few milliseconds behind. Next, we'll decide whether a payment should wait for it.

try.title: Watch a standby follow, then stop it replaying
steps: Start the two servers from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs each server in a container, a sealed box with its own files, and Compose starts several containers from one file. The first start takes about 20 seconds: the primary creates its database, then pg_basebackup copies it for the standby. Look at the processes on both: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary ps -u postgres -o pid,cmd, and the same with standby. docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby bash -c 'cat $PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf' shows what -R wrote.

Open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line client, on each server in its own terminal: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course. Run the session below, switching terminals at each comment. The refunds table holds one row per refund.
Before the count on the standby, predict it: replay is paused, but has the WAL arrived?

sections.h: What COMMIT waits for: synchronous commit, and what each choice can lose
sections.html:
A card reader waits for one answer: the payment is saved. In a database, that answer comes from COMMIT, the command that ends a transaction, a group of changes saved together or not at all. When COMMIT returns, the app tells the reader that the payment went through. So what has happened by the time COMMIT returns?

By default, replication is asynchronous: the primary answers COMMIT as soon as the commit's WAL is on its own disk, and the walsender sends it a moment later. That moment was 2 ms of write_lag in the first Try it. If the primary dies inside it, the standby never gets those commits. After a failover, the switch to the standby, they're gone, though their apps were told they had committed. For a payment the customer's bank already approved, that's money the database no longer knows about.

Synchronous replication closes the gap. Name the standby in synchronous_standby_names on the primary, and every COMMIT waits until that standby confirms. The setting synchronous_commit (default on) chooses what it must confirm:

synchronous_commit COMMIT returns once lost if the primary dies and you fail over
off the WAL is in the primary's memory; a helper process, the WAL writer, saves it within 3 × wal_writer_delay, 600 ms up to 600 ms of commits, even if you never fail over
local the WAL is on the primary's disk whatever the standby hadn't received
remote_write the standby has handed it to its operating system nothing, unless the standby's whole machine crashes too
on the standby has saved it to its disk nothing
remote_apply the standby has replayed it nothing, and a read on the standby sees it at once

With synchronous_standby_names empty, every level from remote_write up behaves like local. The list can name one standby, or say FIRST 1 (s1, s2) for the first connected standby in the list, or ANY 1 (s1, s2) for whichever confirms first.

The price is a round trip to the standby, plus its disk write, on every commit. In this lesson's containers, a commit took about 1.6 ms with local, and 6 to 7 ms when it waited for the standby. With the standby in another building nearby, add about a millisecond; with the primary in Virginia and the standby in Frankfurt, about 70.

Now the trap: a synchronous standby that is down. In One leader, many followers (lesson 1), MySQL, another free database program, fell back to asynchronous when its standby stopped answering. PostgreSQL never does that by itself. In this section's Try it, an INSERT hung for 28 seconds until it was cancelled. statement_timeout, the limit on how long one statement (one SQL command) may run, doesn't end the wait, because its clock stops before the commit starts waiting. A cancel does, with a warning that says exactly what happened: The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated to the standby. The row is on the primary, and everyone can see it.

Synchronous replication delays the answer. It never takes back a commit.

So run two standbys with ANY 1 (s1, s2), so that one can be down. Or let a failover tool switch to asynchronous when the last standby fails, which reopens the gap. And choose per transaction, since SET LOCAL changes a setting for one transaction only: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local for a log of page views, on for the payment.

So far the standby only follows. Next, we'll give it some work, and see why it sometimes refuses.

try.title: Stop the standby: the slot fills the disk, and a synchronous commit hangs
steps: Start the servers if they aren't running (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder) and open psql on the primary (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course). In another terminal, stop the standby: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml stop standby.

Run the first block. It asks how much WAL the slot holds, writes a million rows into a throwaway table, runs a checkpoint and asks again. Then it makes standby1 synchronous and inserts a refund. When the insert hangs, wait about 20 seconds and press Ctrl+C. Predict first: did the refund commit?
Start the standby again (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start standby) and run the last block. Its last three statements put the primary back as it was.

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; SELECT count(*) AS files, pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) AS pg_wal FROM pg_ls_waldir(); CREATE TABLE wal_filler AS SELECT g AS id, md5(g::text) AS pad FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS g; CHECKPOINT; SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; SELECT count(*) AS files, pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) AS pg_wal FROM pg_ls_waldir(); ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); \timing on SET statement_timeout = '5s'; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 250, 'duplicate', now()); -- hangs: Ctrl+C after about 20 seconds SELECT count(*) FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 3 AND amount_minor = 250; BEGIN; SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 260, 'duplicate', now()); COMMIT; -- after: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start standby SELECT application_name, state, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 280, 'duplicate', now()); ALTER SYSTEM RESET synchronous_standby_names; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); DROP TABLE wal_filler;

try.expect:
With the standby stopped, its slot is inactive and holds nothing yet. After a million rows and a checkpoint it holds 92 MB, and pg_wal has grown from 80 MB to 160 MB:

 slot_name | active | wal_status | retained
-----------+--------+------------+----------
 standby1  | f      | reserved   | 0 bytes
 files | pg_wal
-------+--------
     6 | 80 MB
SELECT 1000000
CHECKPOINT
 standby1  | f      | reserved   | 92 MB
    11 | 160 MB

The synchronous INSERT waits, past the 5-second statement_timeout, until you cancel it. psql prints Cancel request sent, then:

WARNING:  canceling wait for synchronous replication due to user request
DETAIL:  The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated to the standby.
INSERT 0 1
Time: 28645.510 ms (00:28.646)
 count
-------
     1

The refund committed: the count finds it. The transaction with SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local commits in 7.8 ms with the standby still down. Right after the standby starts, it shows catchup | potential, and the next commit waits for it to catch up (1.1 s in one run). A few seconds later it shows streaming | sync, and a commit takes about 6.8 ms. Your times will differ; the waiting won't.

sections.h: Reading from a standby, and the reports replay has to cancel
sections.html:
A standby doesn't have to sit idle. With hot_standby = on, the default, it answers read-only queries, questions that read data and change nothing, while it replays. So reports and big exports can run there, and the primary keeps its time for payments. Anything that writes fails with ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction.

Every read on the standby sees the data as of the last record it replayed. So the problems of lesson 3, When followers lag, all apply here: a read just after a write on the primary can miss it. That lesson's fixes are PostgreSQL functions here. Compare pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), how far the standby has replayed, with the LSN of your connection's last commit. Or commit with remote_apply, so the standby has replayed the write before COMMIT returns.

Replay and reads also get in each other's way. When a row is updated or deleted, PostgreSQL keeps its old version for a while, because a transaction that started earlier may still need to read it. (The Transactions track explains why.) VACUUM, a cleanup job on the primary, removes old versions once no transaction on the primary needs them. But the primary knows nothing about the standby's queries. A report on the standby that started at 10:00 may still need a version that the primary removed at 10:05.

Picture a library reader halfway through an old edition, when a clerk comes to remove it for good: the clerk can wait, or take the book away. When the standby reaches the cleanup record in the WAL, it has the same two choices: stop replaying until the report ends, or cancel the report. It waits up to max_standby_streaming_delay, 30 s by default and 5 s in this lesson's Compose file, and then it cancels:

ERROR:  canceling statement due to conflict with recovery
DETAIL:  User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed.

On the standby, pg_stat_database_conflicts counts these cancels. Each fix moves the cost somewhere else. hot_standby_feedback = on makes the standby tell the primary how old its oldest running query is, and VACUUM keeps the versions that query may need. No more cancels, but a 3-hour report now keeps 3 hours of dead rows, old versions nobody else needs, in the primary's tables, and the tables grow. A large max_standby_streaming_delay lets reports finish while the standby falls behind. Then a failover first has to replay the backlog, and every remote_apply commit waits for it.

So give long reports a standby of their own, with a long delay, where lag hurts nobody. Keep the standby you'd fail over to close behind the primary. Next, the primary dies, and that standby has to take over.

try.title: A report on the standby loses to VACUUM on the primary
steps: Start the servers if they aren't running (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder). Open psql on each in its own terminal: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course.
On the primary, give the report something to read: INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 2, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 1000);.

On the standby, start the report. A transaction at the REPEATABLE READ level reads everything as of the moment it began, so it holds on to one snapshot of the data. While it sleeps, delete the rows and run VACUUM on the primary. Predict when the standby's sleep ends.

code.title: psql on the standby and on the primary
code.html: -- standby \timing on BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT count(*) FROM refunds; SELECT pg_sleep(15); -- primary, while the standby sleeps DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 2; VACUUM refunds; -- standby, after the error SELECT count(*) FROM refunds; ROLLBACK; SELECT datname, confl_snapshot, confl_lock FROM pg_stat_database_conflicts WHERE datname = 'course';

try.expect:
The count depends on what earlier Try-its inserted (1,013 rows here). The 15-second sleep ends early, about 5 seconds after the VACUUM:

SELECT pg_sleep(15);
ERROR:  canceling statement due to conflict with recovery
DETAIL:  User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed.
Time: 7045.483 ms (00:07.045)
SELECT count(*) FROM refunds;
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK
 datname | confl_snapshot | confl_lock
---------+----------------+------------
 course  |              1 |          0

The primary's VACUUM removed the deleted versions, the standby's snapshot still needed them, and after max_standby_streaming_delay (5 s here) replay won. The whole transaction is cancelled, not only the one statement, and the conflict is counted as a snapshot conflict.

sections.h: Failover: promoting the standby, and keeping the old primary out
sections.html:
Lesson 1, One leader, many followers, split a failover into three steps: notice that the leader is gone, choose a new one, and send everyone to it. PostgreSQL does none of them: nothing in it notices that the primary is gone. A person or a tool notices, and runs SELECT pg_promote() on the standby. The standby replays the WAL it already has, ends recovery and starts accepting writes. In one run of the Try it, that took 214 ms.

A promoted standby also starts a new timeline, a numbered branch of history. The number is part of every WAL file's name (00000002... after the first promotion), so WAL written after the split never mixes with the old primary's.

With asynchronous replication, a promotion loses every commit the primary confirmed and never sent. The Try it widens that gap on purpose by stopping the standby first. Refund 3333 is lost: its app saw INSERT 0 1, psql's way of saying one row was added, and the new primary has never heard of it.

Then the old primary comes back: its machine restarts, or a broken network link heals. It still believes it's the primary, on timeline 1, and it accepts writes. Two primaries at once is called split brain, and the Try it shows how fast it ruins the data. Both servers hand out refund id 40, one for 4444 and one for 5555, and nothing will ever merge them.

So a failover needs fencing: before the standby takes over, make sure the old primary can't accept writes. Stop it, cut it off the network, or take it out of the load balancer, the program that hands out connections to servers. The PostgreSQL documentation calls this STONITH: "shoot the other node in the head", a node being one server in a group. It's about as gentle as it sounds. To bring the old primary back as a standby, pg_rewind winds its data directory back to the point where the timelines split, and throws away its unsent commits. It needs data checksums, a small check number on every page (on by default since PostgreSQL 18), or the setting wal_log_hints. Otherwise, rebuild it with pg_basebackup.

Programs also have to find the new primary. A Java or Kotlin program talks to PostgreSQL through JDBC, Java's standard database library. PostgreSQL's JDBC driver, pgJDBC, the library that does the talking, can take a list of servers and connect to whichever one accepts writes. Here it's set up through Hikari, a library that keeps connections open for reuse:

HikariConfig().apply {
    jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://db-a:5432,db-b:5432/payments?targetServerType=primary"
    connectionTimeout = 2_000      // during a failover, borrows fail fast and the caller retries
}

By hand, at night, all this is slow and easy to get wrong, so most teams use Patroni, a free program that runs next to each PostgreSQL server. Each running copy, an agent, watches its own server, and the agents need a referee. They use etcd, a small database run on three or more machines, which changes a value only when most of them agree. In etcd sits a leader key, a note that says which server is the primary. The key expires after 30 seconds unless the primary's agent renews it, which it does every 10 seconds (loop_wait). If the primary dies, or loses touch with etcd, the key expires and the standbys' agents race to take it. Because etcd agrees by majority (with Raft, which the Consistency and consensus track builds), exactly one agent wins, and it promotes its server. An agent that can't renew the key turns its own server read-only, and that's the fence.

Cloud companies also sell PostgreSQL that they run for you, such as Amazon RDS and Google Cloud SQL, standby, failover and backups included. The program's side stays yours: short timeouts, and retries for the transactions a failover cuts off.

Every tool so far guards against a server that dies. None of them helps with the opening's cleanup script. Next, we'll take backups.

Nothing in PostgreSQL notices or decides what to do.</text></svg>
frames.say: The primary dies (docker compose kill, like pulling the power cord). Refund 8 exists only on its disk. Nothing in PostgreSQL notices this or picks a successor: a person or a tool must.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The standby is promoted and the commit is lost"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments app</text><rect class="box-dim" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">old primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">down</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">not reachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">new primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">pg_promote(): timeline 2</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="404" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: lost</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">redo done at 0/5003FB0</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">Promoted in 214 ms. Refund 8 never left the old disk: it is lost.</text></svg>
frames.say: Someone runs SELECT pg_promote() on the standby. It replays the WAL it has (redo done at 0/5003FB0), starts a new timeline (selected new timeline ID: 2) and accepts writes, 214 ms later. Refund 8 was confirmed and isn't here: that's what asynchronous replication can lose.

The next refund gets id 40.</text></svg>
frames.say: The app connects to the new primary and keeps working. The next refund gets id 40. The counter that hands out ids logs values ahead in the WAL, and the standby carried on from the last value it had seen logged.

frames.say: The old primary's machine comes back, and PostgreSQL starts as what it was: a primary on timeline 1, with refund 8. A program that still has its address writes refund 5555, and it gets id 40 too. Two servers accept writes and disagree about what refund 40 is. That's split brain, and nothing merges it later.

Rewound, the old primary follows the new one; its refund 8 is gone.</text></svg>
frames.say: The fix is to fence before you promote: stop the old primary or cut it off, so it can't take writes. To bring it back, pg_rewind winds its data directory back to where the timelines split, which throws away refund 8, and it restarts as a standby of the new primary. Patroni fences by turning read-only any primary that can't renew its leader key.

try.title: Promote the standby, lose a refund, then meet two primaries
steps: Start from fresh servers: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v, then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder.

Run the commands below in order. Each psql -c runs one SQL command and prints its answer, and kill stops a container at once, like pulling the power cord. Before the promotion, predict which refunds the new primary will have.
When you're done, docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v deletes both servers.

code.title: in the labs folder
code.html: # 1. a refund that reaches the standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 1111, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" # 2. the standby falls behind (stopped), a refund commits, the primary dies docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml stop standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 3333, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml kill primary # 3. start the standby alone and promote it docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait --no-deps standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT pg_promote()" \ -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 4444, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml logs standby | grep -E "promote|redo done|timeline ID: 2" # 4. the old primary comes back docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start primary docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()" -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 5555, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6"

try.expect:
Refund 7 (1111) reaches the standby. Refund 8 (3333) is confirmed by the primary while the standby is stopped. After the kill and the promotion, the new primary has refund 7 only, and gives the next refund id 40:

 pg_promote
------------
 t
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
 refund_id
-----------
        40
-- the log, prefixes trimmed
LOG:  received promote request
LOG:  redo done at 0/5003FB0 system usage: CPU: user: 0.00 s, system: 0.00 s, elapsed: 3.03 s
LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2

The old primary starts as a primary (pg_is_in_recovery is f, meaning it isn't recovering, so it takes writes) and also gives id 40 to the next refund. The two servers now disagree:

-- old primary
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
         8 |         3333
        40 |         5555
-- new primary
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
        40 |         4444

Refund 8 is the commit asynchronous replication lost. Refund 40 is split brain: two primaries, one id, two different refunds. Ids jump from 8 to 40 because a sequence, the counter that hands out ids, logs 32 values ahead in the WAL, and both servers carried on from the same logged value.

aside.title: Why doesn't PostgreSQL fail over by itself?
aside.html: Because one server can't tell "the primary is dead" from "my own network link is broken". From inside a standby, both look the same: no WAL arrives. If every standby promoted itself after a timeout, one loose cable would give you two primaries, which is the split brain of this section. A safe decision needs a referee that several machines agree on, such as etcd, and PostgreSQL leaves that part to tools like Patroni.

sections.h: Backups: a dump, or a base backup plus the archived log
sections.html:
Run DELETE FROM merchant_fee_schedules without its WHERE clause, the part that says which rows, and every shop's fee rules are gone. (The code calls a shop a merchant.) The standby deletes the same rows a few milliseconds later. So a standby is not a backup. A backup is a copy from the past, and PostgreSQL offers two kinds.

A logical backup is SQL. pg_dump -Fc -d course -f course.dump reads one database as it was at one moment, without blocking anyone who writes. It saves the definition and rows of each table: 33 KB in 0.2 s for the lab's database. pg_restore loads it back, the whole database or one table, even into a later major version. A dump is only as fresh as its last run, though. And restoring one means inserting every row and rebuilding every index, the lookup tables that find rows fast: minutes for gigabytes, hours for terabytes.

A physical backup is the data directory plus the WAL. pg_basebackup takes the copy of the directory, the base backup, exactly as it built the standby. Continuous archiving keeps the WAL. With archive_mode = on, the archiver process runs archive_command for each finished WAL file, a segment of 16 MB. Here the command is test ! -f /archive/%f && cp %p /archive/%f: copy the file into the archive folder, unless one with that name is already there. The primary keeps each segment until the command reports success. On a quiet server a segment can take hours to fill, so set archive_timeout to limit how old the archive can get.

To restore, copy the base backup into an empty data directory, set restore_command to fetch segments back from the archive, create a file called recovery.signal, and start the server. It replays the archived WAL like a standby that knows when to stop. With recovery_target_time, it stops before the first commit after that time, starts a new timeline and opens. That's point-in-time recovery (PITR): last night's base backup, plus the WAL up to the second before the bad DELETE. In the Try it, the restored server logged recovery stopping before commit of transaction 865 and had all 8 fee rules back.

Free tools do the bookkeeping that cp doesn't. pgBackRest, Barman and WAL-G compress, encrypt and check backups, delete old ones on a schedule, and restore in parallel. PostgreSQL 17 added incremental base backups, which copy only the pages that changed (pg_basebackup --incremental, then pg_combinebackup).

A backup you've never restored is a hope. Restore one on a schedule. Restore into a spare server you can throw away, run row counts and a few known queries, and time it. That time is how long you'd be down. The age of the newest archived segment is how much you'd lose. (The deeper section has a checklist for the whole lesson.)

All of this still has one primary taking every write, however far away its customers are. The next lesson asks what changes when more than one server takes writes.

try.title: Undo an accidental DELETE with point-in-time recovery
steps: Start from fresh servers: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v, then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder. Take a base backup into the archive folder, next to the archived WAL: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -u postgres primary pg_basebackup -U sfz -D /archive/base -c fast -P.
Open psql on the primary (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course) and run the session below. Copy the time before_the_mistake prints.

Recover to that time in a third server, restore: TARGET_TIME='2026-11-08 02:30:12.69231+00' docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr up -d --wait restore, with your time in place of this one. Read its log: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr logs restore.

Check the restored server, then copy the rows back to the primary: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr exec -T restore pg_dump -U sfz -d course --data-only -t merchant_fee_schedules | docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -T primary psql -U sfz -d course. Finish with docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr down -v.

code.title: psql on the primary, then on the restored server
code.html: -- primary: a refund after the base backup, then the mistake INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (7, 900, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id; SELECT count(*) FROM merchant_fee_schedules; SELECT now() AS before_the_mistake; SELECT pg_sleep(1); DELETE FROM merchant_fee_schedules; -- the cleanup script forgot its WHERE SELECT pg_switch_wal(); -- close the segment so the archiver copies it now -- restore: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr exec restore psql -U sfz -d course SELECT count(*) FROM merchant_fee_schedules; SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds ORDER BY refund_id DESC LIMIT 2; SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

On the restored server the count is 8, and refund 7 is there: it came from the WAL, not from the older base backup. pg_is_in_recovery is f, so it promoted itself. The copy back prints COPY 8, and the primary has its fee rules again. The base backup took a few seconds. A pg_dump -Fc of the same database is 33 KB and takes 0.2 s, but it could only have brought back last night.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery

mistake: The most common slot mistake is retiring a standby and forgetting its slot. A team switches off the machine of a reporting standby, and does nothing else. Its slot stays on the primary, inactive, with a restart_lsn that never moves again, so no checkpoint may remove WAL after it. pg_wal grows by a day's WAL every day, 50 GB in a busy week, and one night the disk is full, the primary can't write WAL, and it stops. It happens because the slot lives on the primary, and the people who owned the standby never look there. Drop the slot when you retire the standby (SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('reports1')), get an alert when a slot has been inactive for more than a few minutes, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size, or on PostgreSQL 18 idle_replication_slot_timeout, so that a forgotten slot is given up (wal_status becomes lost) before the disk fills.
opening:
Picture a payments company at night. Its database, the program that keeps every card payment, runs on one main computer. A second computer keeps a copy, a few milliseconds behind, in case the first one dies.

At 2:30, a cleanup script runs. It was meant to delete one shop's old fee rules, but someone left out the line that says which shop. Every shop's fee rules are gone, and a few milliseconds later the copy deletes them too, exactly as it was built to.

It's easy to think of a copy as a safety net for every kind of trouble. It catches a computer that dies, but it copies a mistake as faithfully as a payment.

The last lesson, When followers lag, showed what a copy that runs behind does to reads. In this lesson, we'll run the track's ideas on PostgreSQL 18: build a copy, choose what a payment waits for, lose a refund on purpose, and bring the fee rules back from the second before the mistake. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cleanup script at 2:30 and a copy that deleted the same rows a few milliseconds later. A standby protects you from a server that dies, if you fence the old one. Only a copy from the past, a base backup plus the archived WAL, brings the fee rules back.

On a PostgreSQL server you can reach, run SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status FROM pg_replication_slots; and SELECT last_archived_time, failed_count FROM pg_stat_archiver;. Then ask whoever runs it when a backup was last restored, and how long it took.

Next, we'll let a database on another continent take writes too, and find out what happens when two of them change the same row before either has heard from the other.

compare.title: Sending the log to a standby: Oracle Data Guard and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle Data Guard
a.title: Oracle AI Database 26ai
a.html:
transport: redo shipped to the standby
  LOG_ARCHIVE_DEST_2='SERVICE=stby SYNC AFFIRM'
standby: managed recovery applies the redo
  open read-only while applying: Active Data
  Guard, a separately licensed option

protection modes
  MAXIMUM PERFORMANCE   async (the default)
  MAXIMUM AVAILABILITY  sync, but carries on as
                        async if no standby answers
  MAXIMUM PROTECTION    sync; the primary shuts down
                        rather than commit unprotected

failover: the Data Guard broker; Fast-Start
  Failover, where an observer process decides
backups: RMAN, with block-level incrementals

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.html:
transport: WAL streamed by a walsender to the
  standby's walreceiver (primary_conninfo, a slot)
standby: the startup process replays the WAL
  open read-only while replaying: hot_standby,
  on by default

synchronous_standby_names and synchronous_commit
  empty                 async (the default)
  'ANY 1 (s1, s2)', on  sync; commits wait while no
                        listed standby answers, with
                        no automatic fallback
  (Patroni can fall back to async; with
   synchronous_mode_strict it never does)

  with etcd, Consul or ZooKeeper as the referee
backups: pg_basebackup and archive_command,
  pgBackRest or Barman; incrementals since 17

compare.note: Oracle Database is a paid database program that many large companies run, and Data Guard is its standby feature. The idea is the same as PostgreSQL's: send the log of changes (Oracle calls it redo) to a copy and replay it there. Three things differ in practice. Oracle's maximum availability mode drops to asynchronous by itself when no standby answers, while PostgreSQL keeps every commit waiting until someone changes synchronous_standby_names. That's safer for the data and worse for staying up, unless you run two standbys or let Patroni decide. Reading from a standby is built into PostgreSQL, while Oracle sells it as an extra, Active Data Guard. And Oracle ships its own failover referee, the Fast-Start Failover observer, while PostgreSQL leaves that to an outside tool and a store like etcd.

worked.title: Switching to a standby by hand, step by step

steps.say: First make sure the old primary can't take writes, even if it only looks gone from where you stand. Check from two places, then fence it: stop it if you can reach its machine, or take it out of the load balancer and block its port. (pg_isready asks whether a server accepts connections, and ssh runs a command on another machine.)
steps.code: # 1. is it really gone? ask from two networks pg_isready -h db-a -p 5432 # from the app subnet pg_isready -h db-a -p 5432 # from the admin host # fence: stop it, or cut it off ssh db-a 'sudo systemctl stop postgresql' || ssh lb 'disable-backend db-a'

steps.say: Pick the standby with the most WAL on its disk. Compare what each has received, not what each has replayed, because a promotion replays everything received first.
steps.code: -- 2. on each standby SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() AS replayed, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS last_commit_replayed; -- db-b: 2/1A0031C8 db-c: 2/19FF2000 -> promote db-b

steps.say: Promote it and check that it now takes writes. pg_promote waits up to 60 seconds by default and returns false if the promotion didn't finish. Then create a slot for each server that will follow it.
steps.code: -- 3. on db-b SELECT pg_promote(wait => true, wait_seconds => 60); -- t SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); -- f: it is a primary SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('db_c', true); SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('db_a', true);

steps.say: Point the other standby at the new primary. A change to primary_conninfo takes effect when the settings are reloaded, and with recovery_target_timeline = 'latest', the default, the standby follows timeline 2.
steps.code: -- 4. on db-c ALTER SYSTEM SET primary_conninfo = 'host=db-b port=5432 user=replicator application_name=db_c'; ALTER SYSTEM SET primary_slot_name = 'db_c'; SELECT pg_reload_conf();

steps.say: Bring the old primary back as a standby, never as a primary. pg_rewind winds it back to where the timelines split, and whatever it committed after that is thrown away. If you need to know what was lost, look first (the deeper section shows how).
steps.code: # 5. on db-a, PostgreSQL stopped pg_rewind --target-pgdata=/var/lib/postgresql/18/main \ --source-server='host=db-b port=5432 user=postgres dbname=postgres' --progress touch /var/lib/postgresql/18/main/standby.signal # primary_conninfo = 'host=db-b ...' and primary_slot_name = 'db_a' in postgresql.auto.conf, then start it

lab.title: A model of streaming replication: replay, commit waits, slots, failover and point-in-time recovery
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder; they need no Docker. All 27 fail. Streaming.kt gives you a Primary that commits WAL records with LSNs, Standbys copied from a base backup, and a Cluster whose stream sends records the way a walsender does. Read it first.

Exercise 1, Standby.replay: apply each whole record after replayLsn, up to upTo, and never past flushLsn (a standby can't replay what isn't on its disk yet). stream calls it, so most other tests need it.

Exercise 2, Cluster.isAcknowledged: when has the primary answered a COMMIT? With off, local or no synchronous standby, at once. Otherwise, compare the named standbys' write, flush or replay position with the end of the record.

Exercise 3, Primary.checkpoint: mark slots that fell more than maxSlotWalKeepSize behind as lost, then remove the WAL that every remaining slot already has. The tests stop a standby, write 500 commits, and check what the checkpoint keeps.

In Failover.kt, exercise 4 promotes the right standby and lists the confirmed commits it never had, and exercise 5 replays a base backup and an archive up to a target time. Run the tests until all 27 pass.
hints: replay: val limit = minOf(upTo, flushLsn), then loop over wal: continue while record.end <= replayLsn, break at the first record.end > limit, and otherwise applyRecord(record, data) and replayLsn = record.end.

checkpoint: the oldest restartLsn among slots that aren't lost (or currentLsn if there are none) is where the WAL must start, and every record with end <= that position can go. Mark lost slots first, so they don't hold anything.

failover: keep the running standbys within the lag limit, take maxByOrNull { it.flushLsn } (it keeps the first of equals), call its replay(), and the lost commits are acknowledged.filter { it.end > chosen.flushLsn }.

drill.title: A standby from nothing, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write what the primary needs for a new standby, standby2, at 10.20.1.7: the user, the slot and the pg_hba.conf line. Then write the one command on the standby's machine that copies the primary and makes it a standby, and the query on the primary that shows how many bytes the standby's replay is behind.

answer.html: -- on the primary CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD 'long-random-secret'; SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby2', true); -- keeps WAL from now on -- pg_hba.conf, then SELECT pg_reload_conf(); -- hostssl replication replicator 10.20.1.7/32 scram-sha-256 -- on the standby's host, with an empty data directory: -- pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D "$PGDATA" -X stream -S standby2 -R -c fast -- (-R writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo), then start PostgreSQL -- lag, on the primary SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_behind_bytes, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

recap: A standby is a copy of the data directory that never finishes crash recovery: it receives the primary's WAL and replays it onto the same pages. pg_basebackup -R -S builds one: the copy, standby.signal, how to reach the primary, and a slot.

A replication slot makes the primary keep WAL until its standby has it. A slot whose standby is gone keeps WAL until the disk fills, so drop it, watch for inactive slots, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size or PostgreSQL 18's idle_replication_slot_timeout.

By default, COMMIT returns before any standby has the change, so a failover can lose it. With a synchronous standby, synchronous_commit chooses what COMMIT waits for, and a synchronous standby that is down makes every commit wait: run two with ANY 1.
A standby answers reads, but replay cancels a long query that needs row versions the primary has cleaned up. hot_standby_feedback trades the cancels for bigger tables on the primary.
Failover is pg_promote() plus fencing the old primary, so there are never two primaries at once. Patroni does both, with a leader key in etcd that expires unless the primary renews it.

The limit: a standby copies a mistake within milliseconds. Only a backup from the past brings data back: a dump, or a base backup plus the archived WAL, which can restore the second before a bad DELETE. And one primary still takes every write, however far away its customers are.

explain.prompt: A colleague who plans the payments app's features hears "we have a replica" and decides the database can't lose a payment or be down for long. Explain what the copy protects against, what it doesn't, and what it would take to get closer to that promise.
explain.answer: The replica is a second server that copies every change the main one makes, by receiving its log of changes and replaying it. If the main server's machine dies, we can turn the replica into the new main server and be taking payments again within seconds to a minute, so it protects us against long downtime. It doesn't promise that nothing is lost. By default the main server tells the app a payment is saved before the replica has it, so the last fraction of a second of payments can disappear in a failover. Making the replica synchronous closes that gap, at a few milliseconds per payment, but then a dead replica would stop every payment, so we'd need two replicas and wait for whichever answers first. Someone or something also has to decide to switch, and make sure the old main server never comes back as a second one; that's what Patroni or a cloud service does. And the replica copies mistakes at once: a bad DELETE is gone on both within milliseconds. For that we need backups, a base backup plus the archived log, so we can rebuild the database as it was a second before the mistake. We also need to test that restore regularly and know how long it takes.

deeper.html:
A checklist for a payments database on PostgreSQL.

  • at least one standby, with a slot, a limit on what the slot may keep, and an alert when replay falls behind or a slot goes inactive;
  • synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)' over two standbys, or a written decision to accept what asynchronous replication can lose;
  • automatic failover with fencing (Patroni or a cloud service), and a planned switch to the standby, practised regularly;
  • programs that know every server, or one stable address, with short timeouts and retries made safe by a unique key per payment;
  • base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to another site, with archive_timeout set and an alert when archiving fails;
  • a scheduled restore test, with its duration written down.

Two Patroni settings worth knowing. maximum_lag_on_failover keeps standbys that are too far behind out of the race for the leader key (lesson 1's "choose the most up-to-date follower"), and synchronous_mode makes Patroni promote only a synchronous standby. With synchronous_mode_strict, Patroni never falls back to asynchronous, even when no standby is left.

A standby that waits on purpose. With recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h', a standby receives WAL at once but replays each commit only an hour after it happened. When someone runs a bad DELETE, you have an hour to pause its replay (pg_wal_replay_pause()) and copy the rows out, which is much faster than a point-in-time restore of a large database. Never fail over to it.

What did an asynchronous failover lose? The old primary's WAL after the point where the timelines split stays on its disk until you rewind it. Find the split point in the new primary's timeline history file (00000002.history in pg_wal), then run pg_waldump over the old primary's WAL from there. It prints each record, with the transaction ids and the tables they touched, so you can see which commits never reached the standby, and replay them by hand if they matter.

Another kind of cancel. Changing a table's shape on the primary, with ALTER TABLE or DROP TABLE, takes a lock that stops everyone else from using the table. Replaying it on the standby cancels the standby's queries on that table, and pg_stat_database_conflicts counts these as lock conflicts (confl_lock).

Users and their rights. They belong to the whole server, not to one database, so pg_dump skips them. Save them with pg_dumpall --globals-only next to each dump.

Logical replication. This is the row log of Replication logs (lesson 2): CREATE PUBLICATION pay FOR TABLE payments, refunds on the source, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... PUBLICATION pay on the target. The target can run another major version, hold only some tables, and take writes of its own. It needs wal_level = logical, and a replica identity, a way to name each row (usually its primary key), on every table. As of PostgreSQL 18 it copies no changes to table definitions and no sequence values. Use it to upgrade with minutes of downtime, or to feed a reporting database, not as the copy you fail over to.

Standbys of standbys. Cascading replication lets a standby feed other standbys, so a distant data center can have three standbys and only one stream across the ocean. Cascaded standbys are always asynchronous.

Waiting for two of three. Quorum commit goes further than ANY 1: synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)' waits for any two of three standbys, and survives losing one without stopping commits. It looks like Raft's majority rule (the Consistency and consensus track), with one difference. PostgreSQL doesn't elect a new primary from that majority itself, so the promise holds only if the failover tool promotes one of the standbys that confirmed.

Logical slots and failover. Logical replication slots used to stay behind on the old primary at a failover, so subscribers broke. PostgreSQL 17 can copy them to a physical standby (sync_replication_slots = on on the standby, synchronized_standby_slots on the primary), so a subscription carries on from the new primary.

Archiving without a shell command. archive_command runs a shell command per segment. Since PostgreSQL 15, archive_library loads a module instead, which tools such as pgBackRest use for speed. Whichever you use, a failing archive keeps WAL on the primary just as a forgotten slot does, so alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count.

What PostgreSQL 18 (September 2025) changed for replication and recovery:

Area PostgreSQL 18
Slots idle_replication_slot_timeout gives up on slots idle for too long (the first section)
pg_rewind data checksums are on by default in initdb, and pg_rewind needs them
Monitoring pg_stat_io counts WAL reads and writes, including the walreceiver's writes on a standby
Logical replication generated columns can be published (publish_generated_columns); CREATE SUBSCRIPTION streams large transactions in parallel by default; conflicts while applying changes are logged and counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats
Tools pg_createsubscriber --all turns a physical standby into logical replicas of every database; pg_upgrade --swap and kept planner statistics shorten upgrades

PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds logical replication of sequences and a WAIT FOR LSN command for the read-your-writes wait of When followers lag.
